# DAY 1 — PARTICIPANT GUIDE

Observability Foundations & Incident Triage (Module 1\)

# **PRACTICE SCENARIO SET**

* Modules Covered: Observability Fundamentals (MELT); Golden Signals, RED & USE Methodologies; Dashboard Interpretation; Distributed Tracing & Log Correlation; Events & Alert Fundamentals.  
* Scenario Overview: Vendor-neutral observability foundations on the synthetic ShopNow microservices architecture (frontend \-\> checkout \-\> payment \-\> inventory \-\> database): diagnose hidden tail-latency anomalies in Grafana RED dashboards caused by averaging aggregations, trace distributed transactional failures from Jaeger/Zipkin waterfalls to correlated container logs using Trace IDs, and triage simultaneous alert storms using USE methodology to isolate database disk saturation.

# **PRACTICE D1-1 · TEL-D1-101 · 09:00 · Checkout Is Slow but the Dashboard Looks Green**

* Ticket ID: TEL-D1-101 \| Priority: P2: Customer complaints on checkout latency \| Suggested time: 75 min \| Category: Dashboard Troubleshooting \| Platform: SH (Prometheus & Grafana) \| Course Outcome: CO-01.  
* Background Context: Customer support receives escalating reports of sluggish checkout experiences during flash sales. However, the operations NOC reports the executive RED dashboard is completely green with average response time showing a benign 180ms. The participant must investigate the metric aggregation anti-pattern, expose tail latency spikes via p95 histograms, and add the missing Errors panel.  
* Practice Drills: Contrast Arithmetic Mean vs Percentiles (p50, p90, p95, p99); explore why average hides high-latency outliers in bimodal distributions; inspect Prometheus histogram metric types (le buckets); navigate Grafana panel query editor; build missing RED panels.  
* Implementation Overview: 1\. Run ./lab.sh start. 2\. Open Grafana RED Dashboard (http\://localhost:3000). 3\. Inspect 'Payment Duration' panel: notice the query uses 'avg(payment\_duration\_ms)' which flattens a 4500ms outlier spike down to 185ms. 4\. Edit panel query to use histogram percentiles: histogram\_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(payment\_duration\_seconds\_bucket\[5m\])) by (le)) \* 1000\. 5\. Observe the dramatic p95 spike up to 4.8 seconds starting at 08:45 UTC. 6\. Add the missing RED 'Errors' panel: sum(rate(http\_requests\_total{status=\~'5..'}\[5m\])) / sum(rate(http\_requests\_total\[5m\])) \* 100\. 7\. Set error threshold warning at 1% and critical at 5%. 8\. Save dashboard and verify with ./lab.sh check.  
* Your Assignment: Submit: (1) Corrected PromQL query for p95 latency, (2) Exported Grafana dashboard JSON displaying the p95 spike and the new Errors panel, (3) Brief analysis explaining why average masked the incident.  
* Expected Learning Outcome: Master the Golden Signals / RED methodologies, histogram percentile calculations, and dashboard design principles (CO-01).

# **PRACTICE D1-2 · TEL-D1-102 · 11:30 · Orders Fail for One Product: Follow the Trace**

* Ticket ID: TEL-D1-102 \| Priority: P2: Transactions aborted on specific items \| Suggested time: 75 min \| Category: Distributed Tracing \| Platform: SH (Jaeger & Loki) \| Course Outcome: CO-02.  
* Background Context: Orders for a high-value promotional SKU ('PROD-7729') are failing with generic checkout error screens. Downstream microservices report healthy aggregate HTTP 200 rates. The participant must locate the failing distributed trace, analyze the span waterfall, extract the correlation Trace ID, jump to correlated Loki logs, and identify the root cause.  
* Practice Drills: Analyze distributed tracing concepts: Trace ID, Span ID, Parent/Child span relationships, Context Propagation (W3C traceparent headers); identify bottlenecks in span waterfalls; execute trace-to-log correlation queries in Grafana Explore.  
* Implementation Overview: 1\. Execute ./lab.sh start. 2\. In Jaeger UI (http\://localhost:16686) or Grafana Explore, search traces for service 'checkout' with tag 'http.status\_code=500'. 3\. Locate trace 'tr-ord-883912' and open the waterfall view. 4\. Trace the execution: frontend (12ms) \-\> checkout-service (450ms) \-\> inventory-service (430ms, error flag set). 5\. Identify the slowest failing span: 'inventory.reserveStock'. 6\. Copy Trace ID: '4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736'. 7\. Navigate to Loki log explorer: query {app='inventory'} \|= '4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736'. 8\. Discover error log: 'StockReservationException: SKU PROD-7729 warehouse bin locked due to cycle count audit'. 9\. Complete the root cause report and run ./lab.sh check.  
* Your Assignment: Submit: (1) Root and failing child span IDs, (2) Trace ID and matching Loki error log line, (3) Identification of the failing service and warehouse business exception.  
* Expected Learning Outcome: Master distributed trace waterfall analysis, span timing, context propagation, and cross-telemetry correlation between traces and logs (CO-02).

# **PRACTICE D1-3 · TEL-D1-103 · 14:30 · Six Alerts at Shift Start, One Real Problem**

* Ticket ID: TEL-D1-103 \| Priority: P3: Alert storm at shift handoff \| Suggested time: 60 min \| Category: Alert Triage \| Platform: SH (USE Dashboard & Alertmanager) \| Course Outcome: CO-03.  
* Background Context: At the start of the morning operations shift, Alertmanager fires six concurrent alerts across checkout, payments, customer profile, order history, database IOPS, and disk queue length. The operations team is overwhelmed by alert fatigue. The participant must apply the USE methodology (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) to identify the true root resource saturation.  
* Practice Drills: Differentiate Golden Signals, RED, and USE methodologies; diagnose infrastructure saturation (disk I/O queue, thread pool contention, buffer cache misses); classify alerts into causal vs symptomatic; construct an enterprise Problem Card.  
* Implementation Overview: 1\. Run ./lab.sh start. 2\. Inspect active alerts in Alertmanager (http\://localhost:9093): 6 alerts firing. 3\. Group alerts by component: 4 application alerts ('CheckoutSlow', 'PaymentTimeout', 'ProfileQueryDegraded', 'OrderHistory504') and 2 infrastructure alerts ('DiskIOWaitHigh', 'DatabaseQueueSaturation'). 4\. Open the Node & Database USE Dashboard in Grafana. 5\. Inspect Utilization: CPU at 42%, Memory at 65%. 6\. Inspect Saturation: Database disk queue length is pegged at 38 (normal \< 2), disk await is 280ms\! 7\. Inspect Errors: 0 disk hardware errors, confirming pure I/O saturation caused by an unindexed reporting query. 8\. Fill in the standardized enterprise Problem Card: Impacted Services, Primary Saturation Resource, Root Cause Component, and Immediate Mitigating Action. 9\. Run ./lab.sh check.  
* Your Assignment: Submit the completed Problem Card including: Primary Causal Alert, Saturated Resource Metric, List of Symptomatic Cascading Alerts, and Recommended Next Action.  
* Expected Learning Outcome: Master USE methodology, alert storm triage, distinguishing causal root problems from cascading symptoms, and structured incident communication (CO-03).

# **OUTCOMES ACHIEVED — DAY 1**

* Deconstructed the MELT telemetry pillars and correlated metrics, events, logs, and traces during live incidents (CO-01).  
* Identified metric aggregation flaws and implemented accurate p95/p99 latency percentiles and error rates (CO-01).  
* Navigated distributed trace waterfalls, identified latency bottlenecks, and bridged traces to logs using Trace IDs (CO-02).  
* Applied the USE methodology to triage multi-alert storms and pinpoint hardware/infrastructure saturation (CO-03).  
* Drafted enterprise-grade incident Problem Cards with actionable remediation paths (CO-03).

# **TEL-D1-101 — Dashboard Troubleshooting Evidence**

Assignment evidence requested: corrected p95 PromQL, exported dashboard JSON showing the p95 panel and Errors panel, and an explanation of why arithmetic mean masks tail latency.

Implemented dashboard: eight panels are retained. Payment and checkout p95 panels use histogram quantiles; average-latency panels remain for comparison; HTTP 5xx error panels are included. Both payment and checkout error panels have warning threshold 1% and critical threshold 5% in the dashboard JSON.

Corrected p95 query used in the dashboard:  
histogram\_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(payment\_duration\_seconds\_bucket\[5m\])) by (le)) \* 1000

Errors rate logic uses the HTTP 5xx counter divided by total request rate, multiplied by 100\. The dashboard JSON export is a separate submission artifact and should accompany this document.

## **Evidence 101-A — Grafana dashboard after restoration and query updates**

The dashboard shows inventory request count/rate and payment p95/average panels. This is evidence that the dashboard data sources and application scrape targets were restored after the VM restart.

![][image1]

*Evidence file: image(20261112-053502).png*

## **Evidence 101-B — Checkout p95, average and Errors panels**

The checkout p95 panel is approximately 149 ms in the displayed local time window, with the average panel beside it and the checkout HTTP 5xx Errors panel below. The local simulation did not reproduce the guide's expected 4.8-second spike.

![][image2]

*Evidence file: image(20261111-231231).png*

Analysis for submission — Average latency combines all requests into one arithmetic mean. A small number of very slow requests can be diluted by many fast requests, making the dashboard appear healthy. p95 measures the latency below which 95% of requests complete and exposes tail behaviour more clearly. The local test measured checkout p95 at approximately 148.5 ms; the guide's 4.8-second event was not reproduced.

## **TEL-D1-103 — Final Problem Card Assessment Content**

**Impacted services:** Checkout; Payment; Customer Profile; Order History; PostgreSQL Primary.

**Primary causal alert:** DatabaseQueueSaturation.

**Corroborating infrastructure alert:** DiskIOWaitHigh.

**Symptomatic cascading application alerts:** CheckoutSlow; PaymentTimeout; ProfileQueryDegraded; OrderHistory504.

**Saturated resource metrics — provider scenario:** Database disk queue length 38 (normal below 2); disk I/O await 280 ms; CPU 42%; memory 65%; disk hardware errors 0\.

**Suspected root cause component:** Unindexed batch analytics/reporting query causing excessive disk I/O on PostgreSQL Primary.

**Immediate mitigating action:** Identify the unindexed reporting query in the provider PostgreSQL environment. Coordinate with the database owner to terminate the confirmed rogue query (scenario PID 9182), then monitor queue depth and disk await.

Safety/verification note: PID 9182 is a provider-scenario identifier, not a verified local VM process. Do not run kill 9182 on this Ubuntu VM. Provider-side remediation was not performed or independently verified.

The provider scenario's six simultaneous alerts and database saturation values were not recreated locally. The local VM instead showed low host CPU, memory and filesystem utilization; these host measurements must not be substituted for PostgreSQL database queue metrics.
